name: Ettumanoor Mahadeva Temple
deity: The presiding deity is Shiva, revered here in an intense, fierce Aghora aspect. Tradition holds the lingam to be swayambhu, or self-manifested.
period: Ancient origins; major reconstruction in the 16th century
dynasty: Associated historically with the Travancore royal house
summary: Ettumanoor Mahadeva Temple is an ancient Shiva shrine in Kottayam district, celebrated for some of Kerala's finest classical mural paintings. It is renowned for the Ezhara Ponnana, seven and a half golden elephant figures offered to the deity, and stands among the temples linked in the Vaikathashtami observance.

sections.history: The temple has ancient origins that predate reliable written record, and it has long held a place of importance among the Shiva shrines of central Kerala. A significant phase of reconstruction is attributed to the 16th century, which shaped much of the fabric visible today. Over the centuries the temple drew the patronage of the Travancore royal house, an association preserved in the celebrated golden elephant offering. Ettumanoor is also bound to nearby Vaikom and Kaduthuruthy through the Vaikathashtami tradition, by which devotees seek to worship at all three on the same day. This network of devotion, royal patronage, and continuous ritual life has kept the shrine central to the region's religious landscape.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the classic Kerala idiom, built around a circular srikovil, or sanctum, crowned with a conical copper-clad roof. A tall gateway leads through the walled compound into the temple precinct, and traditional woodwork of exceptional quality frames doorways and eaves. The shrine is best known for its mural paintings, counted among the finest classical work surviving in Kerala; the walls carry a much-admired depiction of Nataraja, Shiva in his cosmic dance. Timber carving, laterite and stone masonry, and the measured proportions typical of the region combine into a restrained yet richly detailed whole. The murals and woodwork together make the temple a touchstone of Kerala's artistic heritage.
sections.legends: The presiding lingam is held in tradition to be swayambhu, self-manifested rather than installed by human hands, and Shiva is worshipped here in the fierce Aghora aspect that lends the shrine its particular intensity. The most cherished tradition attached to the temple is that of the Ezhara Ponnana, the seven and a half golden elephants, an offering linked to the Travancore royal house and displayed with great ceremony during the annual festival. Ettumanoor further belongs to the Vaikathashtami observance, in which devotees aspire to worship at Ettumanoor, Vaikom, and Kaduthuruthy within a single day, treating the three shrines as a bound sequence of pilgrimage rather than isolated destinations.
sections.festivals: The foremost occasion at Ettumanoor is the annual Arattu festival, held in the Malayalam month of Kumbham, corresponding to February and March. Spanning about ten days, it is the temple's most important celebration and draws large gatherings of devotees. During the festival the famed Ezhara Ponnana, the seven and a half golden elephants, are brought out in the ceremonial procession known as the Ezharaponnana Ezhunnallippu, one of the most anticipated moments of the temple year. The festival combines ritual worship, traditional music, and processional display, and the appearance of the golden elephants in particular gives the occasion its distinctive character within the temple calendar of central Kerala.
sections.experience: A visit to Ettumanoor rewards quiet attention. The circular sanctum and copper roof anchor a compound where the pace is unhurried, and the true reward lies on the walls, where classical murals repay slow looking. The Nataraja panel, showing Shiva in cosmic dance, is the image most visitors seek out. Traditional lamps, the scent of oil and incense, and the fine woodwork of the doorways create an atmosphere both intimate and grave, in keeping with the fierce aspect in which the deity is worshipped. Early morning and evening worship, when lamps are lit and the sanctum draws devotees, offer the most evocative experience of the shrine.

visit.timings: The temple generally observes traditional morning and evening worship hours, closing during the midday interval as is customary for Kerala shrines. Exact opening times, pooja schedules, and festival timings vary; please verify locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Traditional, modest attire is expected. Men are customarily required to remove upper-body garments before entering the inner precinct, and women should dress conservatively; a mundu or sari is appropriate.
visit.photography: Photography is typically restricted within the inner precinct and near the sanctum, and the murals may not be photographed. Please seek permission and follow the temple staff's guidance.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is at Ettumanoor in Kottayam district, on the Kottayam-Ernakulam route. The nearest railway station is Kottayam, and the nearest airport is Kochi (Cochin International Airport).
